title: How Feng Shui Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explain feng shui, the Chinese practice of arranging buildings and living spaces so that qi (chi) energy flows well. They cover its roots in Chinese Taoism and India's Vastu Shastra, examples of cosmically aligned sites such as Stonehenge and Beijing, and the main schools: classic/form school, compass school (traditional), and Black Hat sect Western feng shui. They explain the five elements (earth, metal, water, wood, fire) and their productive and destructive cycles, yin and yang, and the bagua map with its nine areas and colors, including how Western practitioners align it to the front door while traditional practitioners align it to magnetic north. They close with criticisms of Western feng shui, office tips, and a listener mail about a GED success story.

segments.title: Intro and pronunciation of feng shui
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the episode and debate pronunciation of feng shui (Mandarin vs. Cantonese) and the spelling of Taoism/Daoism.

segments.title: Definition of qi and feng shui
segments.summary: Feng shui is defined as arranging spaces so qi flows well; qi is linked to Taoism and dates to the sixth century BC. Hosts note its popularity in the West since the 1980s and skepticism in China and the East.

segments.title: Origins: India, Vastu Shastra, and cosmically aligned cities
segments.summary: Both China and India claim feng shui origins; Vastu Shastra is an Indian building science, with evidence cited from ancient times. Examples include Stonehenge, Beijing's north-south axis, Washington D.C., and Mexican sites, plus Angkor Wat and the transmission of Vastu via Indian monks.

segments.title: Schools of feng shui
segments.summary: Overview of the main schools: the classic form school from southern China based on landscape, the compass school using magnetism, Chinese astrology and the Bagua map, and the Black Hat sect Western version founded by Thomas Lin Yun and focused on object placement and interior design.

segments.title: Five elements and productive and destructive cycles
segments.summary: Explains the five elements (earth, metal, water, fire, wood) as phases that qi moves through, with productive cycles (fire produces earth, earth produces metal, and so on) and destructive cycles (water douses fire, fire melts metal, earth blocks water, metal chops wood).

segments.title: Yin and yang
segments.summary: Yin and yang are described as opposite states of qi, with yang as light, heat, masculinity and yin as dark, cold, femininity; the symbol's orientation is discussed, with white (yang) on top.

segments.title: The bagua map and placing it in a home
segments.summary: The bagua map is a nine-square grid turned into an octagon-like hexagon with a yellow center; each area has a color and life aspect. Western practitioners align the black career area to the front entrance, while traditional practitioners align it to magnetic north. Examples are given using the hosts' homes and the Lost symbol.

segments.title: Bagua areas, object placement tips, and criticisms
segments.summary: Lists the color and life-area correspondences (black career, blue skills, green family, purple prosperity, red fame, pink love, white children and creativity, gray travel, yellow health) and suggested objects. Discusses criticisms of Western feng shui as interior design, the Disneyland Hong Kong consultation, and the psychology behind it.

segments.title: Office feng shui tips
segments.summary: Tips for arranging an office: face the entrance, use a mirror if not possible, put red behind the chair to block bad qi, and add a fountain or plant or waterfall picture. The hosts note disagreement among practitioners and joke about fluorescent lights.

segments.title: Listener mail: GED success story
segments.summary: A listener named Chris shares that he earned his GED, attended the University of Illinois Chicago, then a PhD in archaeology at Cambridge, and is now a stay-at-home dad.

segments.title: Outro
segments.summary: Hosts ask for listener success stories and point to social media, email, and the website for more information.
